12213               	; 	' ONE PHASE PER PASS, AND NEVER MORE. There are four phases covering an
12214               	; 	' 8 px period, so advancing by the frame delta ALIASES: at fdv 2 the
12215               	; 	' pattern flips between two positions half a period apart and the
12216               	; 	' direction stops being readable, and at fdv 3 the sequence runs 0,3,2,1
12217               	; 	' -- the staircase visibly runs BACKWARDS, carrying its steps down while
12218               	; 	' the rider goes up. That is the wagon-wheel effect, and no amount of
12219               	; 	' phase arithmetic fixes it: a 4-phase cycle can only be stepped by 1.
12220               	; 	'
12221               	; 	' So the ANIMATION is the clock here, and the rider is paced from it --
12222               	; 	' see move_kelly, which advances him by the same fixed 2-and-1 per pass
12223               	; 	' rather than by fdv. Locking the two together is the only way they
12224               	; 	' cannot drift, and it is what "the player moves at the rate the steps
12225               	; 	' carry him" actually means. The cost is that a ride takes 36 passes
12226               	; 	' rather than 36 frames, so it slows down when the loop does -- which is
12227               	; 	' the honest behaviour for a machine that is carrying you.

12241               	; 	#if NES
12242               	; 	' A VBLANK OF ITS OWN, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE-SCREEN FLASH.
12243               	; 	'
12244               	; 	' PPUBUF is not flushed when it is written -- it ACCUMULATES for the whole
12245               	; 	' pass and the NMI empties it in one go, so every VPOKE the radar makes,
12246               	; 	' every HUD digit and this upload all land in the SAME vblank. And the
12247               	; 	' handler's copy loop does not stop when vblank ends: it runs to the end of
12248               	; 	' the descriptor and then writes PPUADDR and both PPUSCROLLs, which
12249               	; 	' mid-frame re-points the PPU's own render address. The rest of that frame
12250               	; 	' is drawn from the wrong place. On screen that is not a dropped tile, it
12251               	; 	' is the ENTIRE PICTURE jumping for a frame -- which is what has been
12252               	; 	' reported, repeatedly, as the screen flashing on an escalator.
12253               	; 	'
12254               	; 	' The arithmetic says it cannot be anything else. NTSC vblank is about
12255               	; 	' 2273 CPU cycles; NMI entry, the flicker test and OAM DMA spend ~560 of
12256               	; 	' them before a single byte is copied. A copy descriptor costs ~50 cycles
12257               	; 	' plus 14 a byte, so these six characters -- 96 bytes, because a tile is
12258               	; 	' SIXTEEN bytes in two bitplanes, not eight -- are ~1400 on their own.
12259               	; 	' That leaves about 270 cycles, or SIX single-byte pokes, for everything
12260               	; 	' else the pass queued. The radar alone beats that whenever a dot moves.
12261               	; 	'
12262               	; 	' Nothing smaller fixes it, because the overrun is per FRAME, not per
12263               	; 	' second: slowing the animation down just makes the bad frames rarer.
12264               	; 	' Splitting the six characters across two frames tears the staircase, and
12265               	; 	' only three of the six have a constant second bitplane, so dropping a
12266               	; 	' plane does not buy a frame's worth either. What DOES work is giving the
12267               	; 	' upload a vblank with nothing else in it: this WAIT flushes the pass's
12268               	; 	' radar and HUD writes, and the descriptor queued below is then almost all
12269               	; 	' the next vblank has to carry -- ~1960 cycles of 2273, inside the window
12270               	; 	' with room to spare.
12271               	; 	'
12272               	; 	' IT COSTS ONE FRAME A PASS, on the two screens that carry a flight and
12273               	; 	' nowhere else -- esc_tick has already returned on the other six. The
12274               	; 	' rider is paced from the animation rather than from the frame delta (see
12275               	; 	' below), so a slower pass slows the ride too and the two cannot drift.
12276               	; 	WAIT
12277               	; 	#endif
12278               	; 	' ONLY THE CELLS THAT MOVE, AND ONLY THIS SCREEN'S. genart.py measures
12279               	; 	' which cells move -- the step cells and the COMPOSITE copies of them
12280               	; 	' that cross a floor -- and groups them WEST then EAST, because only one
12281               	; 	' direction is ever on screen: screen 0 carries a west flight and screen
12282               	; 	' 7 an east one.
12283               	; 	'
12284               	; 	' THIS IS THE ONLY PER-PASS WORK UNIQUE TO THESE TWO SCREENS, and it is
12285               	; 	' `define_char`, which in bitmap mode is LDIRVM3 -- the TRIPLE copy, once
12286               	; 	' per screen third. It therefore costs three times what the character
12287               	; 	' count suggests, which is why these screens run slower than the rest.
12288               	; 	'
12289               	; 	' THE WEST SCREEN USED TO COST HALF AS MUCH AGAIN, because it carries TWO
12290               	; 	' flights: floor 1's crosses into a shop floor and floor 3's into the
12291               	; 	' roof, so it needed both composite sets -- nine characters against the
12292               	; 	' east's six, 216 bytes a pass against 144. It measured 20 passes a
12293               	; 	' second where the east screen managed 24-26. The two sets are
12294               	; 	' PIXEL-IDENTICAL and are never wanted in the same screen THIRD, so they

13099               	;
13100               	; 	' Blank the canvas by WRITING zeros rather than copying 384 of them out
13101               	; 	' of ROM. This runs twice a game -- at setup and on a new Krook -- so a
13102               	; 	' loop costs nothing anybody can perceive, and it hands the fixed area
13103               	; 	' back the best part of half a kilobyte, which is the budget that
13104               	; 	' actually binds. Paced in bursts: a few hundred VDP writes in a single
13105               	; 	' frame are silently dropped (CLAUDE.md 3A).
13106               	; scan_wipe:
13107               cvb_SCAN_WIPE
13108               	; 	' THIS ADDRESS IS A CHARACTER CODE IN DISGUISE, AND IT WENT STALE.
13109               	; 	' 4096 is the pattern table's BOTTOM THIRD -- rows 16-23, which is
13110               	; 	' band 0 and the radar together -- and the canvas characters begin at
13111               	; 	' genart's SCAN_FIRST, so the base is 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8. It was
13112               	; 	' written out by hand as 4096 + 160*8 when SCAN_FIRST was 160; art
13113               	; 	' added later moved SCAN_FIRST to 208 and nothing moved this with it,
13114               	; 	' so the wipe zeroed the 48 characters BELOW the canvas and never
13115               	; 	' touched the canvas at all.
13116               	; 	'
13117               	; 	' Two of those forty-eight are STRUCTURE. ENDWALL is the building's
13118               	; 	' outside wall and SLABP is a pillar's cap. Blanking a pattern in ONE
13119               	; 	' THIRD leaves a character that draws correctly everywhere else and
13120               	; 	' falls back to its own background colour here -- so the GROUND FLOOR's
13121               	; 	' outside wall turned into plain green while the identical wall one
13122               	; 	' storey up was perfect, and the ground floor's pillars lost the brick
13123               	; 	' carried up through the bar above them. ENDWALL appears only on
13124               	; 	' screens 0 and 7, which is exactly why it was reported as happening
13125               	; 	' only on the escalator screens, mirrored side to side.
13126               	; 	'
13127               	; 	' The name table was correct the whole time. Probing it said so, four
13128               	; 	' times. It was the GLYPH that was empty, in one third only -- which a
13129               	; 	' probe that copies the character somewhere else to look at it cannot
13130               	; 	' see, because the copy renders from a different third's pattern.
13131               	; 	'
13132               	; 	' renumber.py rewrites this line from genart.SCAN_FIRST, and
13133               	; 	' checkstruct.py fails the build if the two disagree.
13134               	; 	#swa = 5760			' 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8, the canvas patterns
13135 EA7A 0200  20 	li r0,5760
     EA7C 1680     
13136 EA7E C800  38 	mov r0,@cvb__SWA
     EA80 20E8     
13137               	; 	#if NES
13138               	; 	' AN NES TILE IS SIXTEEN BYTES, NOT EIGHT -- two bitplanes. DERIVED FROM
13139               	; 	' THE LINE ABOVE rather than written out again: renumber.py rewrites that
13140               	; 	' literal out of genart.SCAN_FIRST and checkstruct.py checks it, and a
13141               	; 	' second hand-kept copy of the same number is exactly the fault recorded
13142               	; 	' in the comment above this routine.
13143               	; 	#swa = #swa + #swa

13227               	;
13228               	; 	' THE TWO ACTORS ARE SPRITES; EVERYTHING ELSE IS CHARACTERS.
13229               	; 	'
13230               	; 	' That split is what makes the instrument simple. The floor lines, the
13231               	; 	' flights and the lift car do not move relative to the canvas, so they
13232               	; 	' are pixels in the scanner's own characters and cost nothing to keep.
13233               	; 	' The Kop and the crook DO move, and as sprites they need no colour
13234               	; 	' table, no erase and no priority arithmetic -- they draw over the
13235               	; 	' furniture because sprites always do, and nothing shifts to make room.
13236               	; 	'
13237               	; 	' IT ALSO REMOVED THE BLINK. Kelly flashed because a pixel row of this
13238               	; 	' canvas can only carry one colour, so at close range the two markers
13239               	; 	' merged and the blink was the only thing left to tell them apart. Two
13240               	; 	' sprites are two colours wherever they stand.
13241               	; 	'
13242               	; 	' The furniture is drawn ONCE, by scan_furn. It used to be redrawn every
13243               	; 	' tick because erasing a character-based marker ANDed bits out of
13244               	; 	' whatever it was standing on; there is nothing left to rub it away. The
13245               	; 	' car still redraws itself, because the car actually moves.
13246               	; 	' -- the lift car. IT WAS FLICKERING, and the cause was not the drawing
13247               	; 	' but the ERASING: scan_elev cleared its three cells and put them back
13248               	; 	' every tick, whether or not the car had moved, so several times a second
13249               	; 	' there was a window with the pixels off. A sprite has no erase at all --
13250               	; 	' it is placed, and the VDP does the rest -- and slot 26 sits BELOW the
13251               	; 	' two markers, so the Kop and the crook pass over it without either of
13252               	; 	' them having to know the car exists.

13771               	; 	' ----------------------------------------------------------------------
13772               	; 	' Attributes select a palette per 16x16 quadrant. gennescolor.py derives
13773               	; 	' eight screen tables; draw_screen stages one in nesb, masks fixtures,
13774               	; 	' then uploads all 64 bytes through nes_attrs_put within one vblank.
13775               	; 	' A MESSAGE BOX GOES GOLD ON DARK BLUE, and the caller says which four
13776               	; 	' bytes in #nav.
13777               	; 	'
13778               	; 	' The text's paper is index 1 and its ink index 3 (see the font upload);
13779               	; 	' over the store those are P0's green and gold -- the same green the box is
13780               	; 	' sitting on, which is what made the messages hard to read. P1 is the HUD's
13781               	; 	' palette, dark blue and gold, so pointing the box's attribute bytes at it
13782               	; 	' gives a message the same treatment as the score line.
13783               	; 	'
13784               	; 	' FOUR BYTES AND NOT ONE MORE. An attribute byte covers four characters by
13785               	; 	' four, and the box is sized and placed to cover exactly four of them
13786               	; 	' (gentitle.py BOX_ROW/BOX_COL/BOX_W): byte columns 2..5, which is name
13787               	; 	' columns 8..23. Anything wider would recolour shop floor beside the box.
13788               	; 	'
13789               	; 	' THIS IS A ROUTINE BECAUSE IT WAS WRITTEN OUT TWICE AND MISSED A THIRD
13790               	; 	' TIME. GOT HIM! kept the store's colours while the other boxes changed,
13791               	; 	' and nothing failed -- it is a readable message in the wrong palette.

13793               	; 	' these beside it.

13795               	; 	' Nothing puts them back, because nothing needs to: every path out of a

13920               	; 	' more like it -- four compares, four assignments and four jumps to walk a

13925               	; 	' when it changes and the clock once a second, so the cost is a handful of
13926               	; 	' DIVs a second against roughly sixty bytes of the one budget that is full.

14310               	;
14311               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
14312               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
14313               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
14314               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
14315               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
14316               	; 	'
14317               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
14318               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
14319               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
14320               	; 	'
14321               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
14322               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
14323               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
14324               	; 	'
14325               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
14326               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
14327               	; 	'
14328               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
14329               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units
14330               	; 	' of ten (the prize beside it is `#addv = 5` for fifty points, and the bonus
14331               	; 	' Kop threshold is `#nextk = 1000` for ten thousand), so writing the band in
14332               	; 	' POINTS here shifted every tally one decimal place. Reported from play as
14333               	; 	' "it seems like you awarded 1000 per time unit left" -- exactly right.
14334               	; 	'
14335               	; 	' Nothing failed: 1,000 a unit is a plausible-looking number, the digits
14336               	; 	' all line up, and the only symptom is a score that runs away. The tell is
14337               	; 	' a constant written in a different unit from the routine it is passed to,
14338               	; 	' which is the same class of fault as the px-per-pass speeds in 3A.
14339               	; 	'
14340               	; 	' (This is also why the old comment here said "#bval MUST BE 16-BIT: 300
14341               	; 	' does not fit in a byte". At 10 / 20 / 30 it would, but it stays 16-bit
14342               	; 	' because `#addv` is, and a byte here would buy two bytes of ROM in
14343               	; 	' exchange for a truncation trap the next time somebody edits a band.)

14487               	;
14488               	; 	' AND IT ENDS ON ITS LAST BLIP -- there is no closing accent.
14489               	; 	'
14490               	; 	' Two were tried. The bench's own ending for this variant rose a fourth,
14491               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
14492               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
14493               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
14494               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
14495               	; 	'
14496               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
14497               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
14498               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
14499               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
14500               	; 	' counting stops.
14501               	;
14502               	; 	' `calc_bonus` USED TO LIVE HERE and computed the whole sum by repeated
14503               	; 	' addition, to dodge two hazards at once: `tsec * bmul` is an 8-bit
14504               	; 	' product (a 50-unit capture in the x300 band pays 15,000, six times past
14505               	; 	' a byte), and multiplying properly lands on the MPY/r0 hazard where a
14506               	; 	' 16-bit variable read straight after being multiplied returns the
14507               	; 	' product's high word. Counting the bonus out a unit at a time (above)
14508               	; 	' removes the multiply entirely rather than working around it -- the loop
14509               	; 	' the player watches IS the arithmetic.
14510               	; 	'
14511               	; 	' It also fixed the last-tick case for free: `bn_loop` tests `tsec = 0`
14512               	; 	' on entry, where the old `FOR bi = 1 TO tsec` would have run its body
14513               	; 	' once and paid a full multiplier for no time at all (CLAUDE.md 3A).

14558               	; 	' THE CAST IS NOT TAKEN AWAY YET -- hide_all now runs AFTER the beat.
14559               	; 	'
14560               	; 	' It used to run here, so the moment the clock emptied, Harry and the
14561               	; 	' thing that had just hit him vanished and the sound played over an empty
14562               	; 	' store. The hit that ENDS a round is the worst case: `do_hit` sets tout
14563               	; 	' before the freeze starts and the main loop leaves on the very next pass,
14564               	; 	' so the hit sound gets one tick and everything is already gone.
14565               	; 	'
14566               	; 	' The pause drains the sound; leaving the actors up means it drains over
14567               	; 	' the picture that caused it. Nothing is moving -- the pause ticks sfx_tick
14568               	; 	' and nothing else -- so it is a held tableau, not a frozen game.
14569               	; 	' THE MESSAGE BOX, ON THE GAME SCREEN AND NOT INSTEAD OF IT.
14570               	; 	'
14571               	; 	' It used to CLS before GAME OVER, so the last thing the player saw was
14572               	; 	' the store being deleted and then two words on an empty field -- which
14573               	; 	' reads as the program ending rather than as the game ending. The store
14574               	; 	' stays; the message sits in the middle of it.
14575               	; 	'
14576               	; 	' THE BOX IS THE FONT'S OWN BACKGROUND. Every font character is black on
14577               	; 	' HUD_BG (dark blue), so a row of SPACES is a solid dark blue bar. A blank
14578               	; 	' row above and below the text is a frame for the price of two strings and
14579               	; 	' no new characters, and it reads against the store because nothing else on
14580               	; 	' the playfield is that colour.
14581               	; 	'
14582               	; 	' THIRTEEN WIDE, WHICH IS THE LONGEST MESSAGE PLUS ONE EITHER SIDE.
14583               	; 	' HE GOT AWAY and THE BIPLANE are both eleven. Every string below is padded
14584               	; 	' to exactly thirteen so the box has straight edges, and column 10 puts it
14585               	; 	' at columns 10-22 -- centre 16, the screen's.
14586               	; 	'
14587               	; 	' THE REASON IS ALWAYS ON THE SAME ROW, and that is what lets one layout
14588               	; 	' serve both cases. Losing a life draws three rows around it; losing the

14590               	; 	' rather than replacing it. Printing the reason at a different row for each
14591               	; 	' case would need `PRINT AT` with a variable, and every other PRINT in this
14592               	; 	' program uses a constant.

14594               	; 	' FLUSH THE PASS BEFORE DRAWING A BOX. PPUBUF accumulates for a whole loop
14595               	; 	' pass and is emptied by one NMI, so a message box -- sixty-four cells,
14596               	; 	' sixty-four single-byte descriptors -- was landing in the same vblank as
14597               	; 	' every radar poke and HUD digit the pass had made. The copy then ran past
14598               	; 	' the end of vblank and the tail was DISCARDED at the PPU: a box with
14599               	; 	' characters missing, and the cut moving from run to run, which is why it
14600               	; 	' read as intermittent corruption.
14601               	; 	'
14602               	; 	' One WAIT here empties the buffer; the box's own writes then self-pace,

14862               	;
14863               	; 	' A SOUND STILL PLAYING WHEN THE ROUND ENDS IS ALLOWED TO FINISH.
14864               	; 	'
14865               	; 	' This used to open with a bare `GOSUB snd_off`, which cut it dead. That
14866               	; 	' was not an accident: the decay counters are ticked by the MAIN LOOP, and
14867               	; 	' this pause REPLACES the main loop, so a tone left latched with nothing
14868               	; 	' ticking it hangs for the full ninety frames -- the sticky-audio failure
14869               	; 	' this game has already shipped twice. The answer is to DRAIN the counters
14870               	; 	' rather than to stop silencing.
14871               	; 	'
14872               	; 	' CLEAR THE PENDING LATCHES FIRST. sf* flags are sounds that have not
14873               	; 	' happened yet; left set, the drain below would START one and the pause
14874               	; 	' would end with a fresh note ringing into the next round.
14875               	; 	'
14876               	; 	' THEN TICK sfx_tick WHOLE, not some decay-only part of it. The five
14877               	; 	' counters do not all live in one place: sot, sht and spt are a block at
14878               	; 	' the tail, but spz (the prize arpeggio) and swt (the jump warble) tick up
14879               	; 	' among the code that starts sounds. Draining only the tail would finish a
14880               	; 	' footstep and still cut the arpeggio, which is the one effect with a
14881               	; 	' phrase worth saving. Calling the whole routine also leaves the write
14882               	; 	' order on CHANNEL 2 alone, which spz and spt share.
14883               	; 	'
14884               	; 	' EVERY THIRD FRAME, because the main loop runs about 2.5 frames per pass
14885               	; 	' and this loop waits one frame per turn. Ticking every frame would play
14886               	; 	' everything at two and a half times its tuned speed. Three frames a tick
14887               	; 	' is ~17% slow and gives 30 ticks against the longest effect's 20 passes.
14888               	; 	'
14889               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNTS TICKS, NOT FRAMES, which is what makes the pacing free.
14890               	; 	' Counting 91 frames and firing on every third needs a second counter, an
14891               	; 	' increment and a test -- 48 bytes, on a fixed area with 66 left. Counting
14892               	; 	' 31 TICKS of three WAITs each is the same 93 frames and the same three
14893               	; 	' frames per tick, with none of that. The duration changes by two frames.
14894               	; 	'
14895               	; 	' snd_off still runs at the END, as the backstop for anything the drain
14896               	; 	' did not finish.
14897               	; pause_beat:
14898               cvb_PAUSE_BEAT

15328               cv965
15329               	;
15330               	; 	' THE LOW-TIME WARNING IS SILENT. There was a beep a second under ten, and
15331               	; 	' it was the wrong instrument for the job: the last ten seconds are the
15332               	; 	' busiest part of a round, so a repeating tone arrives exactly when the
15333               	; 	' player most needs to hear the hazards, and it fought the prize arpeggio
15334               	; 	' for channel 2 as well. The flash says the same thing and says it in the
15335               	; 	' place the player is already looking.
15336               	;
15337               	; 	' FOOTSTEPS ARE NOISE, AND ON THE NOISE CHANNEL -- testsounds variant A.
15338               	; 	'
15339               	; 	' They were two alternating TONES on channel 0, which is neither what the
15340               	; 	' original does nor a good use of a channel: the recording says a footstep
15341               	; 	' is a short burst of white noise, and channel 3 was sitting unused while
15342               	; 	' the footsteps and the jump sweep shared channel 0 and had to take turns.
15343               	; 	'
15344               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS RUN D: a SHORT tick at the measured RATE.
15345               	; 	'
15346               	; 	' The two dials are independent and both were tried at the bench. The
15347               	; 	' 2600 plays a 64 ms burst every 165 ms -- six a second -- and variant A
15348               	; 	' copies both. Ten a second was tried on the way here and reads as
15349               	; 	' hurrying rather than running. What D changes is not the cadence but the
15350               	; 	' TICK: two frames rather than four, and a notch louder to carry at half
15351               	; 	' the length. Same six a second, less of it.
15352               	; 	'
15353               	; 	' EIGHT A SECOND, AND THE ACCUMULATOR NOW CARRIES ITS REMAINDER.
15354               	; 	'
15355               	; 	' sfw counted pixels and the trigger did `sfw = 0`, THROWING AWAY whatever
15356               	; 	' was past the threshold. kspd is about four pixels a pass, so a threshold
15357               	; 	' of 17 did not fire at 17 -- it fired at the first multiple past it, about
15358               	; 	' 20, and every rate this was ever set to came out slower than the number
15359               	; 	' said: the "six a second" was 5.2 and the "ten" that read as hurrying was
15360               	; 	' really 8.7. Subtracting the threshold instead keeps the fraction, so the
15361               	; 	' rate is what it claims to be at any walking speed.
15362               	; 	'
15363               	; 	' MEASURED OFF THE COLECOVISION: 14 px, about 7.4 a second.
15364               	; 	'
15365               	; 	' It was 15 px and 6.9 a second, picked between an 8.0 that read as
15366               	; 	' slightly hurried and a 6.1 that read as trudging -- a judgement between
15367               	; 	' two other judgements, with nothing underneath it. The ColecoVision
15368               	; 	' recording settles it: footfalls land every 0.130 s across a twelve-second
15369               	; 	' continuous run, which is 7.7 a second, and that is the one finding in the
15370               	; 	' whole sound analysis the method resolves EXACTLY -- a rhythm rather than a
15371               	; 	' pitch, counted off the RMS track rather than inferred from a spectrum.
15372               	; 	' (colecosounds variant 1A; assets/sfx/sfxref-coleco.md has the working.)
15373               	; 	'
15374               	; 	' 104 px/s over 14 px is 7.43 a second. 13 px would give 8.00, and 7.7 sits
15375               	; 	' almost exactly between them -- so this is the nearer of the two, and it is
15376               	; 	' also the one that does not walk back into the 8.0 that was rejected by ear.
15377               	; 	'
15378               	; 	' WHY THE GAME KEEPS A DISTANCE AND THE BENCH KEEPS A CADENCE. The bench
15379               	; 	' plays a fixed eight frames between steps because it has no walking to tie
15380               	; 	' them to; the game accumulates PIXELS TRAVELLED, so the feet keep time with
15381               	; 	' the legs when he is slowed or stopped. Matching "7.4 a second" therefore
15382               	; 	' means matching it AT HIS WALKING SPEED, and assumes the ColecoVision's
15383               	; 	' crook walks at ours -- which the recording cannot confirm.
15384               	; 	'
15385               	; 	' The dial is this one constant and the subtraction below, which must stay
15386               	; 	' threshold + 1 or the carry is wrong.
15387               	; 	'
15388               	; 	' SOT = 2 IS THE SHORTEST TICK THERE IS, and 1 is SILENCE. The decay block
15389               	; 	' below runs LATER IN THE SAME sfx_tick, so a count of 1 is decremented to
15390               	; 	' zero on the pass that set it and the note-off fires before the sound has
15391               	; 	' lasted any time at all. 2 survives to the next pass, which is one pass of
15392               	; 	' sound -- about 42 ms against the bench's 33, as close as a per-pass timer
15393               	; 	' gets, and the reason the bench and the game cannot sound identical.
15394               	; 	'
15395               	; 	' Register 4 is white noise at the fastest rate.
15396               	; 	'
15397               	; 	' VOLUME 9, WHICH IS UNDER EVERYTHING ELSE ON PURPOSE. The hit, the prize
15398               	; 	' and the jump are 12 and 13, and they happen ONCE; footsteps play for the
15399               	; 	' whole round. At 13 they were level with the events they are supposed to
15400               	; 	' sit beneath, so the effects that carry information had nothing to stand
15401               	; 	' out from. The tone version was 7 for the same reason -- noise does read
15402               	; 	' quieter than a tone at the same number, which is why this is 9 and not
15403               	; 	' back to 7.
15404               	; 	IF sfw > 13 THEN
15405 F5E8 D020  34 	movb @cvb_SFW,r0
     F5EA 2210

15728               	;
15729               	; 	' EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE IS ASSEMBLED INTO BANK 1, so the INCLUDE order
15730               	; 	' is load-bearing and nothing but data may follow it.
15731               	; 	'
15732               	; 	' THE FONT IS NOW IN THE BANK TOO, and it used to be deliberately outside:
15733               	; 	' keeping one readable thing in bank 0 means a bank-selection mistake shows
15734               	; 	' as "text survives, art does not" rather than a uniformly blank screen,
15735               	; 	' which is a genuinely useful thing to have when a bank goes wrong.
15736               	; 	'
15737               	; 	' THE FONT HAS A BANK OF ITS OWN, and the reason is not its size.
15738               	; 	'
15739               	; 	' Bank 1 was FULL -- six spare bytes of 8,192 -- which shut the door on
15740               	; 	' moving anything else out of the fixed area, and the fixed area is the
15741               	; 	' only budget that cannot be grown (linkticart writes exactly three
15742               	; 	' loader pages and discards the rest; they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
15743               	; 	' >A000, not cart ROM). A second bank costs a bigger cart -- five pages
15744               	; 	' round up to eight, so 32 KB becomes 64 KB -- and buys back the ability
15745               	; 	' to keep evacuating data out of code.
15746               	; 	'
15747               	; 	' THE FONT IS THE RIGHT TENANT because it is read ONCE. Two DEFINEs copy
15748               	; 	' it into VRAM at setup and nothing looks at it again, so it is the only
15749               	; 	' block here that can sit on a page which is not permanently mapped. See
15750               	; 	' setup_font: bank 2 is selected for those two statements and bank 1 for
15751               	; 	' the whole of the rest of the program.
15752               	; 	'
15753               	; 	' EVERYTHING ELSE STAYS IN BANK 1, because everything else is read during
15754               	; 	' play -- art on a screen crossing, templates on a band blit, the lookup
15755               	; 	' tables every pass. One permanently-mapped bank for all of it means
15756               	; 	' there is no switch to miss.
15757               	; 	#if TI994A
15758               	; 	BANK 2
15759      07BC     BANK_0_FREE:	EQU >fffe-$

16804               	;
16805               	; 	' NO ALPHA LOCK CALIBRATION, AND THERE USED TO BE ONE.
16806               	; 	'
16807               	; 	' The premise was that ALPHA LOCK shares a line with the joystick's
16808               	; 	' VERTICAL axis, so a latched key reports a direction that is never
16809               	; 	' released -- fatal here, where down is the duck and up is the lift. The
16810               	; 	' guard sampled the axis for forty frames before listening and then
16811               	; 	' ignored any direction that had been held for essentially all of them.
16812               	; 	'
16813               	; 	' IT WAS REMOVED BECAUSE THE PREMISE DOES NOT HOLD UP.
16814               	; 	'
16815               	; 	'   * CLAUDE.md claimed every other game here dodged the problem by not
16816               	; 	'     reading up/down. EIGHT of them do read it -- Adventire, Astiroids,
16817               	; 	'     HardHatMack, Ms. Pac-Man, RallyX, Structris, UFO, Bust-A-Bobble --
16818               	; 	'     and not one has a calibration or has ever shown the fault.
16819               	; 	'   * It never fired on the machine this is developed on: the notice it
16820               	; 	'     prints when it detects a stuck axis has never appeared.
16821               	; 	'   * The original evidence was that the game "came up and would not
16822               	; 	'     start" -- and the first version BLOCKED until the axis cleared. That
16823               	; 	'     symptom is indistinguishable from the several input bugs since found
16824               	; 	'     and fixed for real: keys arriving at a screen that was not listening
16825               	; 	'     yet. The diagnosis was probably one of those.
16826               	; 	'
16827               	; 	' It also cost two bugs of its own: forty frames of a drawn but deaf title
16828               	; 	' screen, which swallowed the first digit of 8-3-8, and a wrong theory
16829               	; 	' about keyboard noise that led to a filter which ate real presses.
16830               	; 	'
16831               	; 	' If a stuck axis ever does appear it will be obvious -- the player will
16832               	; 	' duck or ride the lift without asking -- and the guard is in the history.
16833               	;
16834               	; title_input:
16835               cvb_TITLE_INPUT
16836               	; 	' THE PROMPT IS PRINTED HERE, NOT WITH THE REST OF THE TITLE, because
16837               	; 	' this is the moment the game starts listening -- and it is a whole
16838               	; 	' second after the title appears.
16839               	; 	'
16840               	; 	' title_draw runs early on purpose (DESIGN.md 0d-nonies) so the screen
16841               	; 	' arrives instead of filling in, but setup_rest, init_tables and the
16842               	; 	' ALPHA LOCK sample all run AFTER it. For about a second the title is up,
16843               	; 	' finished, and completely deaf. A player types 8-3-8 into that window and
16844               	; 	' the first digit lands in nothing -- then a following 3-8 completes the
16845               	; 	' code, because the 8 they typed second is still standing as state. That
16846               	; 	' is exactly how it was reported, twice, and it is not noise: it is the
16847               	; 	' screen lying about being ready.
16848               	; 	'
16849               	; 	' RallyX and Bust-A-Bobble never showed this because they draw their

16882 678A A684     	data wait
16883               	; 	' THE MARQUEE CHASES WHILE THE TITLE WAITS.
16884               	; 	'
16885               	; 	' ONLY TWO CHARACTERS CHANGE PER STEP. At any moment exactly one of the
16886               	; 	' four lamps is blank; a step lights the one that was blank and blanks the
16887               	; 	' next one round. Redefining all four would be twice the work for the same
16888               	; 	' picture.
16889               	; 	'
16890               	; 	' IT IS BELOW THE INPUT READS, deliberately. This loop's history is input
16891               	; 	' bugs -- a screen that was drawn but not listening, a keypress eaten by a
16892               	; 	' stability filter -- so nothing that is merely decoration goes in front of
16893               	; 	' the polling. A dropped frame of animation is invisible; a dropped
16894               	; 	' keypress is what took three sessions to find.
16895               	; 	' `bphs` IS WHICH LAMP IS DARK, and a step is: light that one, move on,
16896               	; 	' darken the next. The character number is arithmetic rather than a
16897               	; 	' four-way branch -- DEFINE CHAR takes an expression, so the whole chase
16898               	; 	' is two calls and no `IF` ladder. The ladder version was eight DEFINE
16899               	; 	' CHARs across four branches and cost about three hundred bytes for the
16900               	; 	' same picture.
16901               	; 	'
16902               	; 	' TWO CALLS, NOT FIVE. Lighting all four and then darkening one is the
16903               	; 	' same result and reads more simply, but two separate DEFINEs can have a
16904               	; 	' vblank between them, so the sign would show ALL lamps lit for a frame
16905               	; 	' every step -- a flash rather than a chase. Only ever changing the two
16906               	; 	' lamps that actually change cannot do that.
16907               	; 	bfr = bfr - 1
16908 678C D020  34 	movb @cvb_BFR,r0

16925               	; 		' QUEUED, NOT BLANKED -- AND THIS IS WHAT MADE THE TITLE FLASH.
16926               	; 		'
16927               	; 		' nes_def turns rendering OFF and waits for a vblank the NMI
16928               	; 		' therefore never services, so the game's own WAIT then waits for
16929               	; 		' the one after: about two frames with the picture switched off.
16930               	; 		' Twice a marquee step, for ever, on the one screen the player
16931               	; 		' looks at longest. It reads as the whole title flashing, not as
16932               	; 		' the bulbs animating.
16933               	; 		'
16934               	; 		' nes_escd hands the NMI a copy descriptor instead. Nothing is
16935               	; 		' turned off and no frame is lost -- and both bulbs land in the
16936               	; 		' SAME vblank, which also settles the worry in the note above:
16937               	; 		' there is no longer a frame in which all four lamps are lit.

16971               	; 		' A SECOND STAGING AREA, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE MARQUEE BUG.
16972               	; 		'
16973               	; 		' nes_escd does NOT copy anything. It builds the tile into the RAM
16974               	; 		' buffer `#nesb` and hands the NMI a five-byte descriptor holding a
16975               	; 		' POINTER to it; the copy happens at the next vblank. Both marquee
16976               	; 		' writes happen in the same pass, so with one buffer the darken call
16977               	; 		' overwrote the staged LIT bytes before the NMI had read either --
16978               	; 		' and then BOTH descriptors copied bulb_off.
16979               	; 		'
16980               	; 		' So every step darkened two lamps and lit none, and the sign walked
16981               	; 		' itself out: "it animates a little bit and goes out". Nothing fails,
16982               	; 		' because both writes are perfectly valid and land exactly where they
16983               	; 		' were addressed -- they just carry the same sixteen bytes.
16984               	; 		'
16985               	; 		' The lit call staged at nesb(0); this one stages sixteen bytes up.
16986               	; 		' nesb is 96 bytes for the escalator's six characters and the
16987               	; 		' escalator never runs on the title screen, so the room is free. The
16988               	; 		' pointer is put back immediately: esc_tick stages at offset 0 and
16989               	; 		' would otherwise write its six characters one tile off.
16990               	; 		#nesb = #nesb + 16
16991               	; 		#nsrc = VARPTR bulb_off(0)
16992               	; 		nchr = bcode

17174               	;
17175               	; 	' 8-3-8 IS EDGE-TRIGGERED AND ANY STRAY DIGIT RESETS IT (see title_wait).
17176               	; 	'
17177               	; 	' It used to read cont1.key raw every pass and test only for the digit it
17178               	; 	' wanted next. That worked -- but only because 8-3-8 ALTERNATES, so holding
17179               	; 	' 8 cannot advance past the first step. It is an accident of the sequence
17180               	; 	' rather than a design, and it had two costs: 8,5,3,9,8 opened this page as
17181               	; 	' readily as 8,3,8, and a key that READS as held for many frames got a free
17182               	; 	' walk through the state machine.
17183               	; 	'
17184               	; 	' That second one is not hypothetical on this machine. ALPHA LOCK shorts a
17185               	; 	' keyboard line -- and Classic99 defaults to invertcaps, so it reads DOWN
17186               	; 	' with the host's Caps Lock UP -- and this page was reached twice from
17187               	; 	' single keypresses while testing an unrelated change.
17188               	; 	'
17189               	; 	' The reset is the DEFAULT rather than a test for a particular wrong digit:
17190               	; 	' Bust-A-Bobble resets only on a stray 3 and still lets 8,5,3,8 through.
17191               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------------- 838 setup page
17192               	; 	' ======================================================================
17193               	; 	' A NEW GAME / A NEW KROOK
17194               	; 	' ======================================================================
17195               	;
17196               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- MOVED TO BANK 2
17197               	; 	' setup_font and init_tables run ONCE, at power-on, and read nothing from
17198               	; 	' bank 1 -- so on the TI they live here, in bank 2, and the caller selects
17199               	; 	' bank 2 around the GOSUB. They moved to make room for the TI music player
17200               	; 	' (title music, ~1.2 KB of runtime in the fixed area): with it, the
17201               	; 	' UNOPTIMISED first assembly ran past >FFFF and xas99 rejected branches
17202               	; 	' before shortbranches.py could run (CLAUDE.md 3A, TI short-branch note).
17203               	; 	' A routine placed here must not BANK SELECT (it would unmap itself) and
17204               	; 	' must not read bank 1: init_tables' one bank-1 read, jarc_tbl, stayed
17205               	; 	' behind as init_jarc. On ColecoVision and NES this is ordinary code.
17206               	; setup_font:

17237               	;
17238               	; 	#if NES
17239               	; 	' THE NES'S TWO STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCES, SETTLED ONCE, HERE.
17240               	; 	'
17241               	; 	' 1. WHERE THE PATTERNS LIVE. In 8x16 sprite mode the sprite pattern table
17242               	; 	'    is chosen by bit 0 of each OAM tile byte and the PPUCTRL bit is
17243               	; 	'    ignored -- and every pattern number in this game is a multiple of
17244               	; 	'    four, so that bit is always 0 and the sprites are nailed to $0000.
17245               	; 	'    nes_bgbank therefore moves the BACKGROUND to $1000 rather than trying
17246               	; 	'    to move the sprites, which also lands the background patterns at
17247               	; 	'    address 4096, exactly where the TMS bitmap mode's third screen third
17248               	; 	'    had them -- so the radar's pattern writes need a stride and nothing
17249               	; 	'    else.
17250               	; 	'
17251               	; 	' 2. COLOUR DOES NOT MAP AND IS NOT PRETENDED TO. The NES colours in 16x16
17252               	; 	'    attribute blocks; this game colours per character, two colours a
17253               	; 	'    cell. So the store is drawn in ONE ink and the actors get four
17254               	; 	'    palettes, picked by the low two bits of the colour argument the
17255               	; 	'    SPRITE statements already pass -- 1 (black) -> dark grey, 4/8 (blue)
17256               	; 	'    -> blue, 14 (grey) -> grey, 11/15 (skin, white) -> white. Nothing in
17257               	; 	'    the game source has to know.
17258               	; 	ASM JSR nes_bgbank
17259               	; 	ASM JSR nes_apuon
17260               	;
17261               	; 	' Grey is shared index 0 during gameplay. Other indices are per region.
17262               	; 	' gennescolor.py assigns P3 only to counter quadrants, retaining green
17263               	; 	' wall and gold floor colours. Fixtures with black outlines use P0.
17264               	; 	PALETTE 1,26			' P0: green, black, gold
17265               	; 	PALETTE 2,15			' black escalators and fixture outlines
17266               	; 	PALETTE 3,40
17267               	; 	PALETTE 5,1			' P1 HUD/upper skyline: blue, pink, gold
17268               	; 	PALETTE 6,36
17269               	; 	PALETTE 7,40
17270               	; 	PALETTE 9,38			' P2 lower skyline: orange, black, gold
17271               	; 	PALETTE 10,1			' unused skyline index 2: navy message bottom border
17272               	; 	PALETTE 11,40
17273               	; 	PALETTE 13,26			' P3 counters: green, blue, gold
17274               	; 	PALETTE 14,1			' same navy in counter quadrants
17275               	; 	PALETTE 15,40
17276               	;
17277               	; 	' AND FOUR FOR THE ACTORS, which DO get one each because a sprite carries
17278               	; 	' its own palette number. nes_spal maps the TMS colour every SPRITE
17279               	; 	' statement already passes onto these four.
17280               	; 	PALETTE 17,18			' 0 -- blue   Kelly's trousers
17281               	; 	PALETTE 21,15			' 1 -- black  hats, Harry's stripes, the Kop's dot.
17282               	; 					' FIFTEEN, NOT ZERO: on this palette $0F is
17283               	; 					' black and $00 is a dark GREY, so every hat
17284               	; 					' and every stripe was coming out grey.
17285               	; 	PALETTE 22,23			' black sprite palette, index 2: brown suitcase outline
17286               	; 	PALETTE 25,39			' 2 -- skin   faces and the biplane
17287               	; 	PALETTE 26,16			' 2 colour 2 -- GREY, the lift car on the radar
17288               	; 	' AND THE BALL IS RED, which it already is on the TI: C_BALL is TMS 8,
17289               	; 	' medium red. nes_spal sends that to sprite palette 2, and palette 2's
17290               	; 	' colour ONE is the skin tone -- so on this machine the ball came out the
17291               	; 	' same pale orange as a face.
17292               	; 	'
17293               	; 	' A sprite here is ONE bitplane, so its pixels are whichever index the
17294               	; 	' upload writes and the OAM byte only chooses the palette. The lift car on
17295               	; 	' the radar already solved this: it is uploaded with `nink = 2` and reads
17296               	; 	' palette 2's second entry. The ball does the same with the THIRD, which
17297               	; 	' nothing else uses.
17298               	; 	PALETTE 27,22			' 2 colour 3 -- RED, the bouncing balls
17299               	; 	PALETTE 29,48			' 3 -- white  Harry, the carts, the lift car
17300               	;
17301               	; 	#endif
17302               	; 	#if TI994A
17303               	; 	#else
17304               	; 	nespw = 2			' NES/Coleco start on a 2-frame pass
17305               	; 	#endif
17306               	;
17307               	; 	' THE ONE AND ONLY BANK SWITCH THE PROGRAM EVER MAKES, and it happens
17308               	; 	' here, before the first frame.
17309               	; 	'
17310               	; 	' There are two data banks now. Bank 1 holds everything read while the
17311               	; 	' game is running -- sprite and store art, the templates, the lookup
17312               	; 	' tables -- and it is selected at the end of this routine and never
17313               	; 	' changed again, so every VARPTR/PEEK read in the program is reading a
17314               	; 	' page that is permanently mapped. That is the property that makes
17315               	; 	' banking safe here: a missed BANK SELECT returns bytes from the wrong
17316               	; 	' page with no error at build or run time, so the safest number of
17317               	; 	' switches during play is none.
17318               	; 	'
17319               	; 	' Bank 2 exists to hold data that is read ONCE, at setup, and never
17320               	; 	' again. The font is exactly that: two DEFINEs copy it into VRAM and
17321               	; 	' nothing reads font_bits or font_col for the rest of the run. So it can
17322               	; 	' live on a page that is mapped for the length of those two statements.
17323               	; 	'
17324               	; 	' IF THIS EVER FAILS IT FAILS LOUDLY. Select the wrong bank here and the
17325               	; 	' font is garbage on the title screen, immediately and unmistakably --
17326               	; 	' which is the same diagnostic the font used to provide by staying out of
17327               	; 	' the banks altogether, recovered for free.
17328               	;
17329               	; 	#if NES
17330               	; 	' THE FONT IS SENT WITH A COLOUR TABLE SO ITS PAPER IS NOT THE BACKDROP.
17331               	; 	'
17332               	; 	' With `#ncol = 0` the uploader puts ink `nink` on index 0 -- the UNIVERSAL
17333               	; 	' backdrop, black in the game -- so every character of text sat in its own
17334               	; 	' black box. The score line was a black strip across the top of a blue sky.
17335               	; 	'
17336               	; 	' Index 0 cannot be set per region (it is one colour for the whole screen),
17337               	; 	' so the only way to give text a ground is to put its PAPER on another

17613               	; 	' THE JUMP ARC IS A TABLE, not integration. That makes the 14 px apex a
17614               	; 	' property of the data rather than of a fixed-point velocity that has to

17619               	; 	' frames that touched 14 for only four, which made every jump a timing
17620               	; 	' test rather than a decision -- you had to leave the ground on exactly
17621               	; 	' the right frame or clip the thing you were jumping. Widening the
17622               	; 	' plateau rather than raising the apex keeps the ball arithmetic in
17623               	; 	' DESIGN.md 5a intact (the apex is what that depends on) while making the
17624               	; 	' window forgiving: the player still has to CHOOSE to jump, but no longer
17625               	; 	' has to be frame-perfect about it.

17661               	;
17662               	; 	' THE FONT'S COLOUR TABLE WAS 472 BYTES OF ONE REPEATED VALUE, which is a
17663               	; 	' fifth of what the fixed area had left. DEFINE COLOR copies such a table
17664               	; 	' out of ROM into all three screen thirds; writing the constant straight
17665               	; 	' into the colour table does the same job for the price of a loop, and
17666               	; 	' the loop runs once, at boot.
17667               	; 	'
17668               	; 	' The colour table is at >2000 and the VDP mirrors it once per screen
17669               	; 	' third, >800 apart. Both numbers were read out of the GENERATED assembly
17670               	; 	' -- define_color's `ai r0,>2000` and LDIRVM3's `ai r0,>0800` -- rather
17671               	; 	' than assumed, because a wrong base here would paint over the pattern
17672               	; 	' table and the failure would look like corrupt artwork.
17673               	; 	'
17674               	; 	' Paced: a few hundred VDP writes in one frame are silently dropped.
17675               	; 	' THE SCANNER'S COLOURS ARE THREE BLOCKS REPEATED SIXTEEN TIMES EACH, so
17676               	; 	' the table shipped 384 bytes to say 24 bytes' worth. Same trick as the
17677               	; 	' font: write the colour table directly. >2000 is the colour table's base
17678               	; 	' and >800 the stride between screen thirds -- the same layout DEFINE COLOR
17679               	; 	' walks for us in setup_font, which this cannot use because it is cheaper to
17680               	; 	' expand 24 bytes here than to ship 384 in the bank.
17681               	; 	' NOTHING IS UNDER THE GROUND FLOOR, SO NOTHING SHOULD BE GREEN THERE.
17682               	; 	' A floor bar is five pixels of yellow over three of the green air
17683               	; 	' belonging to the floor BELOW it (see SLAB), which is right for three of
17684               	; 	' the four bars and wrong for the last one: below floor 0 there is no
17685               	; 	' floor, only the scanner, and the green read as a strip of shop with
17686               	; 	' nothing in it.
17687               	; 	'
17688               	; 	' NO NEW CHARACTER IS NEEDED, BECAUSE THE COLOUR TABLE HAS THREE COPIES
17689               	; 	' -- one per eight screen rows -- and the bands land such that each bar
17690               	; 	' sits in a different third:
17691               	; 	'
17692               	; 	'     band 0 roof   rows  1-5    bar row  5   third 0
17693               	; 	'     band 1        rows  6-10   bar row 10   third 1
17694               	; 	'     band 2        rows 11-15   bar row 15   third 1
17695               	; 	'     band 3 GROUND rows 16-20   bar row 20   third 2
17696               	; 	'
17697               	; 	' so recolouring SLAB in third 2 alone reaches the ground floor's bar and
17698               	; 	' nothing else. The same third also holds the scanner, but the scanner
17699               	; 	' does not use these characters. This is the same mechanism that once hid
17700               	; 	' a bug for months (CLAUDE.md 3A, the blanked-in-one-third note) used
17701               	; 	' deliberately for once.
17702               	; 	'
17703               	; 	' Only the three bottom lines change, and only their BACKGROUND: SLAB has
17704               	; 	' no ink there and SLABE's brick keeps its grey.
17705               	;
17706               	; 	INCLUDE "font.bas"
17707               	; 	' Keystone Kapers font -- GENERATED by assets/genfont.py. Do not edit; regenerate.
17708               	; 	'
17709               	; 	' Characters 32-90 (59 of them), 8 bytes each = 472 bytes. Williams' cabinet face:
17710               	; 	' heavy, squared, flat terminals, no serifs -- drawn 5x7 inside the 8x8 cell so a
17711               	; 	' blank column at the right and a blank row at the bottom keep it legible.
17712               	; 	'
17713               	; 	' Loaded with DEFINE CHAR 32,59,font_bits. The run must be CONTIGUOUS, so slots
17714               	; 	' with no glyph emit blanks rather than being skipped -- a gap would shift every
17715               	; 	' letter after it.
17716               	;
17717               	; font_bits:
17718               cvb_FONT_BITS

17837               	;
17838               	; 	' THE COLOUR TABLE, 472 bytes of the same value ($B4 = light yellow ink on dark blue).
17839               	; 	'
17840               	; 	' Loaded with DEFINE COLOR 32,59,font_col, which is ONE synchronous call that
17841               	; 	' writes all three screen thirds (define_color always does the LDIRVM3 triple
17842               	; 	' copy). It replaced a VPOKE loop that wrote this one value 1,416 times paced by
17843               	; 	' 24 WAITs -- the largest scripted delay in the boot, and the reason the title
17844               	; 	' screen used to fill in visibly rather than appearing at once.
17845               	; 	'
17846               	; 	' EIGHT BYTES PER CHARACTER, not one. Supply fewer and DEFINE COLOR reads
17847               	; 	' whatever follows in ROM as colour data, with no error at build or run time.
17848               	;
17849               	; #if NES
17850               	; 	' NES uses nes_fcol; omit this identical 472-byte TMS colour table.
17851               	; #else
17852               	; font_col:
17853               cvb_FONT_COL

18857               	; 	INCLUDE "art.bas"
18858               	; 	' Keystone Kapers art -- GENERATED by assets/genart.py. Do not edit; regenerate.
18859               	; 	'
18860               	; 	' EVERY SPRITE IS 16x16: sprite size and magnification are GLOBAL on the
18861               	; 	' TMS9918, so small objects are drawn small INSIDE a 16x16 box rather than
18862               	; 	' being small sprites.
18863               	; 	'
18864               	; 	' EVERY 8-PX OBJECT SITS IN ROWS 8-15 OF ITS BOX, ducked Kelly included, so
18865               	; 	' one rule places them all: bottom edge = y + 16, and a thing resting on the
18866               	; 	' floor is at y = FLOORY - 16.
18867               	; 	'
18868               	; 	' Sprite bytes are QUADRANT-ORDERED: 16 rows of the left half, then 16 of
18869               	; 	' the right. Every block is an EVEN number of bytes -- an odd DATA BYTE run
18870               	; 	' silently misaligns every word table after it (CLAUDE.md 3A).
18871               	;
18872               	; spr_kelly:	' Kelly: RIGHT hat/face/two merged run bodies/two FREE slots/duck hat/face/body, then the same LEFT (+36). The run bodies carry tunic AND legs, so a frame is one sprite, and standing is run frame 1. Patterns 0..68
18873               cvb_SPR_KELLY

20104               	; 	INCLUDE "store.bas"
20105               	; 	' Keystone Kapers store -- GENERATED by assets/genstore.py. Do not edit.
20106               	; 	'
20107               	; 	' EIGHT band templates of 5 rows x 32 cols (160 bytes each) plus a 32-byte
20108               	; 	' index over (level, screen). The whole 8-screen, 4-level building is about
20109               	; 	' 1.3 KB instead of the 5,120 bytes it would cost to store literally.
20110               	; 	'
20111               	; 	' All eight templates are ONE contiguous block under ONE label, so a band
20112               	; 	' blit is
20113               	; 	'     SCREEN stor_tpl, tpl*160, toprow*32, 32, 5, 32
20114               	; 	' with no label ladder -- SCREEN needs a literal label and a label cannot be
20115               	; 	' chosen by a variable, which is why RallyX needed a 4-way IF over its maze
20116               	; 	' tables. One block sidesteps it.
20117               	; 	'
20118               	; 	' 160 is EVEN, so this cannot leave the location counter odd and misalign
20119               	; 	' the word tables defined after it.
20120               	; 	'
20121               	; 	' template ids:
20122               	; 	'   0 T_AISLE_A
20123               	; 	'   1 T_AISLE_B
20124               	; 	'   2 T_ESC_W
20125               	; 	'   3 T_ESC_E
20126               	; 	'   4 T_ELEV
20127               	; 	'   5 T_ROOF0
20128               	; 	'   6 T_ROOF1
20129               	; 	'   7 T_ROOF2
20130               	; 	'   8 T_ROOF3
20131               	; 	'   9 T_ROOF4
20132               	; 	'   10 T_ROOF5
20133               	; 	'   11 T_ROOF6
20134               	; 	'   12 T_ROOF7
20135               	; 	'   13 T_END_W
20136               	; 	'   14 T_END_E
20137               	;
20138               	; stor_tpl:	' 15 templates x 160 bytes
20139               cvb_STOR_TPL

20754               	;
20755               	; 	' THE SKYLINE'S LAST BAND WITHOUT ITS YELLOW, high nibble ink, low nibble
20756               	; 	' paper, one byte a scan line -- the same shape genart emits into
20757               	; 	' store_col. SKY2 is white-on-9 throughout instead of turning to paper 10
20758               	; 	' at row 4; BLDGL holds its blue one row longer and then meets its own
20759               	; 	' grey wall. Both are the generated bytes with 10 replaced by 9 and
20760               	; 	' nothing else changed. See setup_rest.
20761               	; #if NES
20762               	; nes_sky2c:
20763               	; 	DATA BYTE $F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9
20764               	; nes_bldlc:
20765               	; 	DATA BYTE $B9,$B9,$B9,$B9,$B9,$BE,$BE,$BE
20766               	; #endif
20767               	;
20768               	; 	' THE IN-GAME FONT'S COLOUR, one byte a scan line and eight a character for
20769               	; 	' all 59 of them. $B4 is light yellow on dark blue -- ink index 3, paper index 1 --
20770               	; 	' and which colours those are is then the attribute table's business, per
20771               	; 	' region: dark blue behind the HUD, the store's green behind a message box.
20772               	; 	'
20773               	; 	' 472 bytes of one repeated value. That reads like waste and is the cheap
20774               	; 	' option: ROM is three budgets here and this is not the scarce one, while
20775               	; 	' the alternative is a second font (impossible -- only eleven free codes)
20776               	; 	' or a new uploader parameter (no RAM -- two bytes left).
